title: perf: kosaraju_strongly_connected_components 7.2x slower than nx — delegated; needs native kernel emitting nx's exact 2-phase order
description: Profiled 2026-06-12 (cc), gn_graph n=200/500: fnx 1.145ms/2.897ms vs nx 0.149ms/0.377ms = 7.2-7.7x slower. fnx DELEGATES via _call_networkx_for_parity (full fnx->nx conversion) because the native fnx-algorithms kosaraju_strongly_connected_components (crates/fnx-algorithms/src/lib.rs:27121) emits SCCs in a DIFFERENT sequence than nx (it does phase1=postorder-on-ORIGINAL then phase2=DFS-on-reversed + sorts each component; nx does phase1=dfs_postorder on G.REVERSE -> phase2=reverse-pop + dfs_preorder on ORIGINAL). SCC SETS are correct (0 partition mismatches) but SEQUENCE differs and is NOT a simple reversal (50/80 reversed-seq mismatches). KEY FINDING: in-process port using fnx's OWN dfs_postorder_nodes(G.reverse())+dfs_preorder_nodes is byte-exact vs nx (0/100) BUT 2x SLOWER than the delegation (fnx dfs/reverse primitives + per-root PyO3 too slow) — so pure-Python is a DEAD END. FIX: rewrite the native fnx-algorithms kernel to faithfully mirror nx's 2-phase order (postorder-on-reverse via predecessors in node-iteration order -> reverse-pop -> preorder-on-original via successors), drop the per-component sort (Python wraps as set). Compose native dfs_postorder_nodes_directed/dfs_preorder_nodes_directed (lib.rs:17455/17516) to match nx dfs order. Then de-delegate the wrapper (__init__.py:18316) to the native kernel. Target 7.2x slower -> parity/faster. Clean files: fnx-algorithms/lib.rs (kernel) — but BLOCKED while peer active across the Rust substrate. Same order issue affects sister strongly_connected_components (also delegated, br-r37-c1-2vdtt). Byte-exact reference harness: /tmp/test_kos2.py logic.
close_reason: SHIPPED fde375500: rewrote native fnx-algorithms kosaraju kernel to mirror nx's exact 2-phase emission order (postorder on G.reverse -> reverse-pop -> forward preorder pruned at seen), de-delegated wrapper for source=None. gn_graph n=200: 1.145ms->0.089ms (~12.9x self-speedup), 7.2x-slower-than-nx -> 1.65x FASTER; n=500 1.42x faster. title: perf(to_directed/to_undirected/deepcopy): Python copy.deepcopy of immutable-valued attr dicts dominates (0.71-0.80x vs nx)
description: MEASURED+PROFILED (cc verify phase, fresh build): to_directed 0.75x, to_undirected 0.71x, deepcopy-family vs nx on attributed gnp(2000). cProfile of to_directed (20 iters): _native_to_directed_deepcopy self 0.497s, then Python copy.deepcopy 918k calls = 1.38s of 1.88s total (_deepcopy_dict 0.293s, _keep_alive 0.150s, id() 1.76M calls). ROOT CAUSE: the native to_directed deep-copies every node/edge attr dict via Python copy.deepcopy — even for dicts whose values are all IMMUTABLE (str/int/float), where deepcopy==shallow copy (verified: both fnx+nx are DEEP for nested lists, so the contract needs deep, but for immutable values a Rust/shallow clone is equivalent). nx pays copy.deepcopy too but has no Rust round-trip; fnx adds the _native round-trip on top. LEVER: in deepcopy_py_dict / _native_to_directed_deepcopy, fast-path attr dicts with all-immutable values to a Rust dict clone (or shallow copy), falling back to Python copy.deepcopy ONLY when a value is mutable/nested (correctness: memo semantics for shared nested objects). Could make to_directed BEAT nx (skip copy.deepcopy entirely for the common immutable-attr case). BENCH: to_directed(attributed gnp(2000)) vs nx (currently 0.75x). CONFORMANCE: deepcopy guard exists (test_deepcopy_conformance_guard); MUST preserve deep semantics for nested mutable + memo sharing. fnx-python binding (cc/CrimsonRiver territory); builds now allowed. This is THE construction-substrate frontier (also tbh4q).

title: perf(views): len(G.adj) 0.8077x — the deficit is a PyO3 bound-method call where nx has a C dict len; closing it needs a NATIVE AdjacencyView.__len__ slot
description:
Measured by OliveDesert 2026-08-08 on ELF 675707ac (post br-r37-c1-7faiu), balanced-square substrate, every ratio carrying its own dual A/A null (all nulls 0.9991-1.0009), load 7.2 of 64.

DECOMPOSITION (500 len() calls per timed unit; ns are per single len()):
  len(G.adj) public          nx 72.1 ns   fnx 89.3 ns   -> 0.8077x CI [0.8057, 0.8102]
  raw: len(dict) vs native_len()  nx 24.7 ns   fnx 35.2 ns   -> 0.7049x CI [0.7022, 0.7067]
  fnx public vs fnx raw      -> 2.5628x  (fnx's Python __len__ frame costs 54.3 ns)
  nx  public vs nx raw       -> 2.9252x  (nx's  Python __len__ frame costs 47.4 ns)

So the 17.2 ns deficit splits: 10.5 ns is the raw call (PyO3 bound-method call vs a C len() on a dict) and 6.7 ns is fnx's heavier __len__ body. BOTH sides are dominated by the Python __len__ frame (47-54 ns of a 72-89 ns call), which is Mapping-protocol cost neither library escapes today.

  nx  AtlasView.__len__:      return len(self._atlas)              # attr load + C dict len
  fnx AdjacencyView.__len__:  n = self._fnx_native_len; if n is not None: return n()   # attr load + None test + PyO3 call

THE OBVIOUS FIX IS WRONG — TESTED, REFUTED, DO NOT RETRY IT. Swapping native_len() for len(self._fnx_owner) would replace the PyO3 method call with the graph's C length slot and recover most of the 10.5 ns. It is a SEMANTICS CHANGE. Demonstration on HEAD: build a 3-node fnx Graph, then assign G._node = <a 5-node dict>. Then len(G) == 5 and G.number_of_nodes() == 5, but av._fnx_native_len() == 3 and len(G.adj) == 3. native_len correctly tracks the ADJACENCY owner count while len(owner) tracks the private-aware node count; under a private _node override they legitimately differ, and nx agrees with 3 because its AdjacencyView is built over _adj, not _node. Swapping would silently return 5.

THE REAL LEVER, and why it is not one commit: make the adjacency view a NATIVE type whose __len__ is a C slot. crates/fnx-python/src/views.rs:990 already has an AdjacencyView pyclass with fn __len__ at :996, but G.adj returns the PYTHON franken_networkx.AdjacencyView (a _Mapping subclass) because that is where the nx-parity getitem caching, iteration order and row semantics live. A native __len__ slot would skip the ~54 ns Python frame ENTIRELY and land around 35 ns against nx's 72 ns — i.e. roughly 2x, a WIN rather than a 0.81x loss. That is a view-class migration, not a one-line lever, and it must preserve: the _fnx_atlas_cache (nodes_seq, {node: AtlasView}) contract, the native-iter binding, filtered/reverse/reconstructed/snapshot views that pass no native_len, and the private-override behaviour proved above.

DO NOT attack the None test alone: it is worth ~3-5 ns of 17.2 on an 89.3 ns call, i.e. 3-6%, which sits at the across-run drift floor (measured at +1.1% to +2.8% on negative controls in br-r37-c1-7faiu) and is not separably measurable by a two-invocation before/after.
close_reason: Implementation landed as br-r37-c1-5gam7: G.adj inherits the native __len__ C slot; len(G.adj) 0.8077x -> 1.6548x CI [1.6447,1.6641] vs live nx same-invocation, A/A nulls 1.0004/1.0047, unanimous 4/4.

title: to_directed(as_view) / to_undirected(as_view) dispatch silently bypassed (sibling of br-r37-c1-hfug2)
description:
Phase 4 of the view-dispatch audit. G.to_directed(as_view=True) and G.to_undirected(as_view=True) return dynamic subclasses of _ConversionGraphViewBase + DiGraph/Graph (synthesized via type() at module load).

These isinstance-pass the canonical-type check in _coerce_arg_to_fnx_graph (they ARE DiGraph/Graph by MRO) but their Rust inner graph still holds the SOURCE adjacency. Algorithms that read the inner directly bypass the view's directionality flip and silently produce wrong answers.

Verified bug:
  fd = fnx.DiGraph(); fd.add_edges_from([(0,1),(1,2),(2,0)])  # directed cycle
  fu_view = fd.to_undirected(as_view=True)
  fnx.is_connected(fu_view)
  # returned False; nx returns True
  fnx.shortest_path_length(fu_view, 0, 2)
  # raised NetworkXNoPath; nx returns 1 (via the undirected 0-2 edge)

Fix: insert isinstance check for _ConversionGraphViewBase BEFORE the canonical-type check in _coerce_arg_to_fnx_graph. Materialize via _from_nx_graph (which deserializes the view's edges() — already in the correctly-transformed orientation — into a fresh fnx graph).

Verified post-fix: is_connected, shortest_path_length, pagerank all match nx exactly on both directed→undirected and undirected→directed view conversions. 17517 Python tests pass (17516 → 17517 with the new regression-lock test).
notes: Fixed in same commit by adding _ConversionGraphViewBase isinstance check to _coerce_arg_to_fnx_graph.

title: BFS algorithms need integer-indexed optimization
description:
Performance issue: has_path is 6.85x slower than NetworkX, shortest_path is 4x slower.

Root cause: BFS implementations use HashSet<&str> for visited tracking and neighbors_iter(str) for traversal instead of Vec<bool> and integer indices.

Compare to bfs_edges which uses integer indices and is 1.8x faster than nx.

Optimization needed:
1. Convert to Vec<bool> visited tracking with get_node_index()
2. Use neighbors_indices() for O(1) integer-based traversal
3. Remove ComplexityWitness allocations in hot paths (or make them optional)

Affected functions:
- has_path / has_path_directed / has_path_generic
- shortest_path / shortest_path_directed
- single_source_shortest_path (still 2.9x slower after BFS-order fix)

See br-r37-c1-bapbi for reference implementation pattern.
close_reason: Optimized has_path (2.7x faster), shortest_path (2.3x faster) with integer indices. sssp (paths) improved from 13.5x to 3x slower - remaining slowness is inherent path cloning

title: POLLUTION: test_subpackage_namespace_parity root_mirror/overlay star-exports fail under import-order in broad namespace run
description: test_subpackage_namespace_parity::test_root_mirror_modules_define_star_exports_like_networkx + test_overlay_modules_... PASS in isolation but FAIL when run with the broad 'namespace or module_parity' test set (import-order pollution, same CLASS as the 0ouoj dispersion clobber). NOT caused by cc's tests (verified: my coexistence/interop/routing/clobber tests + the subpackage test = 47 passed). fnx.algorithms.__all__ is STABLE under submodule imports (0 divergence vs nx exports even after importing 14 submodules), so the polluted root-mirror module is a DIFFERENT one (the test iterates ROOT_MIRROR_MODULE_EXPORTS over several modules). Likely a lazy-__all__/dir() import-order fragility in some root-mirror module whose dir() grows when a peer test imports its submodules. Owner of test_subpackage_namespace_parity should bisect: which ROOT_MIRROR module's __all__ diverges + which test triggers it. cc's namespace/__all__ work (2qsqf/8wp6u) is not implicated. Found via session-test health check (run files together to surface import-order bugs).
notes: ROOT CAUSE PINNED (cc): the diverging item is 'tests'. test_subpackage_namespace_parity._expected_exports(nx.algorithms) returns dir(nx.algorithms) (nx.algorithms has no __all__), which INCLUDES 'tests' AFTER test_package_child_module_parity's pkgutil.walk_packages imports networkx.algorithms.tests (lazy). fnx.algorithms.__all__ CORRECTLY excludes 'tests' (8wp6u pkgutil-append filters name!='tests'). So fnx is RIGHT (you don't expose .tests as public API); the TEST expectation is fragile. FIX (in test_subpackage_namespace_parity._expected_exports, a PEER test -- not cc-owned): filter 'tests' (and '_'-prefixed) from the dir()-based expected set, matching what __all__ derivation excludes -> exp = {n for n in dir(m) if not n.startswith('_') and n!='tests'}. One-line test fix. NOT an fnx runtime/product bug (fnx.algorithms.__all__ is correct + stable). cc 8wp6u/2qsqf not implicated; this is the test's nx-side expectation not excluding the tests package.

title: test: oracle-free shortest-path algorithm-agreement metamorphic coverage
description: Cross-checks Dijkstra==Bellman-Ford, triangle inequality, BFS-hop<=weighted-distance, undirected symmetry across 3 independent shortest-path implementations. 180 cases. Catches single-algorithm bugs via cross-algorithm disagreement.
close_reason: A NON-DUPLICATIVE DELTA REMAINED, contrary to the 2026-08-04 comment - and the gap is in the bead own headline claim. The docstring promises agreement "across 3 independent shortest-path implementations", but only TWO are ever compared for equality: Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford. The third named source is unweighted BFS, which supplies a BOUND (hop count <= weighted distance), not an equality - so no third algorithm was ever required to produce the same distances. I added two that do: Floyd-Warshall, an all-pairs method from a different algorithmic family, and Johnson, whose returned PATHS I re-weight from the graph to get lengths. Both agree with Dijkstra on 70/70 draws, verified before writing. The claim in the docstring is now true rather than aspirational. NEGATIVE WEIGHTS, the capability that makes Bellman-Ford genuinely independent of Dijkstra rather than a slower duplicate: the random family draws weights in 1..9, so it was never exercised. Added a witness where the cheaper route is cheaper ONLY because of a negative edge (0-1-2 costs 2 against a direct edge of 5). Added the negative-CYCLE contract too: shortest paths are undefined there and Bellman-Ford raises NetworkXUnbounded in fnx and in live networkx 3.6.1 alike, rather than returning an answer. DELIBERATELY NOT ASSERTED: Dijkstra behaviour on negative weights. It happens to return the correct answer on my witness, but Dijkstra on negative edges is undefined territory, not a contract - pinning it would freeze an accident and could break on any legitimate implementation change. I checked that fnx and nx currently agree there and chose to leave it unpinned rather than bank the coincidence. DEAD GUARD: the "if g.degree(src) == 0: skip" guard in both pre-existing sweeps fires 0 times of 70 at this density; my new sweep omits it rather than copying it. Evidence: file 180 -> 252 passed, no skips; 302 passed across the shortest-path family (all_pairs_shortest_path_parity, astar_yen). Crate-scoped and inline with a timeout cap; no background jobs left running. Committed cf9c2ce31, pushed to main then master separately after a fast-forward check. Test-only, no Rust touched, no CGSE surface.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SATISFIED AT 140 CASES — AND STRENGTHENING IT FOUND A REAL DIVERGENCE (CopperCliff, 2026-08-08).

tests/python/test_graph_operators_set_algebra.py already existed and matched this bead: complement
(parity + K_n partition + disjointness), compose=union, intersection, difference,
symmetric_difference (each with parity AND its law), and cartesian/tensor/strong product size
parity, at 50 + 50 + 40 = 140 cases — exactly the figure specified. I checked before writing.

TWO ASSERTIONS THAT COULD NOT FAIL FOR THE REASON THEY WERE WRITTEN.

  1. Everything went through `_edge_set(g)`, which is a SET of SORTED pairs. That discards the node
  set (a graph carrying extra isolates has the same edge set) and the iteration order (the CGSE
  contract) in one step.
  2. The product test compared only number_of_nodes() and number_of_edges(). Two graphs of the same
  size and completely different shape pass it.

MEASURED BEFORE ASSERTING, 50 identically-built seeded pairs, fnx vs live nx 3.6.1:

    operator             node-order div.   edge-ORDER div.
    complement                 0 / 50            0 / 50
    compose                    0 / 50            0 / 50
    intersection               0 / 50            0 / 50
    difference                 0 / 50            0 / 50
    symmetric_difference       0 / 50            0 / 50
    cartesian_product          0 / 50           49 / 50
    tensor_product             0 / 50           38 / 50
    strong_product             0 / 50           38 / 50

THE FIVE SET-ALGEBRA OPERATORS ARE ORDER-EXACT and are now locked as such — new
test_set_algebra_operators_preserve_iteration_order asserts list(nodes()) and list(edges()) for all
five, 50 seeds.

THE THREE PRODUCTS ARE NOT. Same edge SET, same node ORDER, different edge SEQUENCE. Filed as
br-r37-c1-28lwc with the per-operator counts and a concrete instance (seed 0, cartesian: the first
two edges are transposed and the sixth differs — fnx emits a node's G-edge and H-edge blocks in the
opposite order to nx). This was invisible to the previous assertions by construction, which is the
point: sorting is what hid it.

WHAT I DID NOT DO. I did not assert product edge order, because it would red the suite over a known
divergence that is now separately tracked, and I did not "fix" the products, because that is a
change to native kernels that needs its own investigation (the ledger's byte-identical claims for
the 2026-07 product batch levers are fnx-before vs fnx-after, NOT fnx vs nx, so they neither
implicate nor exonerate those levers — 28lwc says so explicitly rather than guessing). The product
test now asserts node ORDER and the edge SET, which is strictly stronger than counts, and carries an
explicit comment stating that edge order is deliberately unasserted and why. Turning that comment
into an assertion is 28lwc's acceptance test.

Cases 140 -> 190. File: 190 passed. Full Python suite: 50828 passed, 1081 skipped, 0 FAILED.

title: _fnx_to_nx conversion: O(N·E) topo sort + per-edge lookups (~3x speedup)
description:
_fnx_to_nx() is on the hot path for every fnx algorithm that delegates to nx for parity (louvain_communities, label_propagation_communities, many minor wrappers). On a 200-node 1000-edge graph it took 21ms, with two components dominating:

(1) _topo_emit_edges_by_adj used a 'while emitted_count < total_edges: for u in nodes_order' pattern with list.pop(0) — O(N) inner loop per edge emitted, so O(N·E) worst case. 11ms on the test graph.
(2) dict(fg.edges[u, v]) per edge for attr lookup. 5ms.

Fix: rewrite topo emit with a 'ready' deque (each node enqueued when its queue-front is reciprocally matched), O(N + E) total. Pre-fetch all (u, v, attrs) into a frozenset-keyed dict (undirected) or tuple-keyed dict (directed; collapsing 0,1 ↔ 1,0 would corrupt asymmetric attrs like mutual_weight). Combined: 21ms -> 6.7ms (~3x faster overall, 6.4x faster on the topo emit alone).

Verified: all 17506 Python tests pass. Re-running the perf-parity sweep: louvain wrapper 24ms -> 12ms; LPA wrapper 20ms -> 8.7ms.
notes: Fixed in same commit. Ready-queue O(N+E) topo emit + frozenset/tuple-keyed attr cache. Direct/undirected branches diverge correctly (mutual_weight test would have caught the bug if I'd unified them — added that as a regression test path).

title: perf-gate: clause 3 vetoes a reproducible 4.4x effect ~25% of the time — a single 21-round A/A null draw is too fragile a control
description:
DEMONSTRATION EVIDENCE (the AGENTS.md standard (a) for a gate defect: same ELF, effect reproduces,
pass/fail verdict moves). br-r37-c1-p80x1.14, minimum_branching, preregistered fixture with input
and complete-output SHA-256 both matching, live nx 3.6.1, 21 rounds, dual A/A nulls, 8 independent
repetitions, host thinkstation1, ELF sha256 7545dd0aec67244002f1441cc99cd41d2fc77a220ff6e7378f0831a58af24a36,
taskset -c 40-43, loadavg 8.22:

  effect  4.2831-4.4494x (median 4.4119x, 3.9% spread) — stable across all 8 runs
  clause 1 (CI excludes 1)              passed 8/8
  clause 2 (effect > 2x null half-width) passed 8/8
  clause 3 (worst null median bias <= 0.02) FAILED 2/8
  verdict: 6/8 decidable, 2/8 UNDECIDABLE

The two vetoes came from different arms (run2 nx null 0.9772, run7 fnx null 0.9574), so this is not
a property of either implementation. Subject-side explanations were checked and ruled out: no
degradation across 20 consecutive calls, a fresh graph is not faster, gc.collect() is neutral, and
calibrate() returns inner=1 deterministically for both arms. It is sampling noise in a single
21-round median under host contention.

WHY THIS MATTERS: clause 3 is doing real work — it is what catches a genuinely biased measurement —
but as written it is a single draw with no retry, so a large stable effect has roughly a 25% chance
of being thrown away per attempt on a contended host. That is very likely a large share of the
'no current admissible ratio' rows under br-r37-c1-p80x1, and it means a retry that changes nothing
about the code can flip the verdict, which is exactly the property a gate must not have.

DO NOT simply raise MAX_NULL_MEDIAN_BIAS. That is the loosening AGENTS.md names. Candidate fixes
that keep the clause's power:
  * re-draw the null on failure (bounded retries) and require the MEDIAN of null medians to clear —
    turns one noisy draw into an estimate;
  * pool both arms' nulls instead of taking the worst single median;
  * require the null's bias to be small relative to the candidate's effect rather than absolute
    (0.0426 bias against a 3.44 effect deviation is not a threat to the verdict).

BLOCKING PREDICATE (the AGENTS.md standard (b), which this bead cannot close without): publish the
integrity check. Run the full claim-incumbent suite under the current clause 3 and under the
candidate clause 3, and report how many previously-vetoed rows become decidable AND the WIN vs LOSE
split of exactly those rows. A change that admits only wins is a loosening, not a fix, and must be
reverted. Do not land a gate change without that table.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SIDE EVIDENCE + A CHEAPER FIRST TEST (OliveDesert, 2026-08-08). Not closing the bead — the blocking predicate is untouched. Two things that bear on it.

CAVEAT FIRST, so this is weighed correctly: my numbers come from a DIFFERENT harness, the balanced-square same-invocation substrate used across this session's ledger rows, not from perf_harness.py. Different round count, different slot layout, different workloads. It is suggestive of host behaviour, NOT a substitute for the suite run this bead requires.

WHAT ~70 A/A NULL DRAWS ON THIS HOST LOOK LIKE AT 41 ROUNDS. Across 17 balanced-square invocations this session (karate, preferential_attachment/jaccard, the has_node/has_edge/degree canonical-key sweep before and after, len(G.adj) decomposition and ceiling, add_edge, the k7-vs-k8 cliff), every arm carried its own A/A null. Essentially all landed inside 0.992-1.004, i.e. a bias below 0.008, comfortably inside MAX_NULL_MEDIAN_BIAS = 0.02.

Exactly ONE draw exceeded the clause-3 bound: 0.9756 (bias 0.0244), in a len(G.adj) before/after run taken at one-minute load 22.29. In that same run the null CI half-width widened to 0.0553 and the candidate row came back NOT DECIDABLE. I discarded that run and re-took it at load 5.41, where the nulls returned to 1.0012/1.0004 and every row decided. So on the one occasion clause 3 fired here, it fired on a genuinely corrupted measurement and it was RIGHT. That is a point in the clause's favour and should be weighed against the 2/8 vetoes in the demonstration.

THE DIFFERENCE THAT LOOKS CAUSAL, AND IT IS NOT THE THRESHOLD. The demonstration ran 21 rounds on 4 cores (taskset -c 40-43) at loadavg 8.22. My runs were 41 rounds on 8 cores (taskset -c 40-47) at loads 1.9-7.9. Same host, same class of measurement, and the null bias distribution is visibly tighter. That is what one expects if the failure mode is precisely what the bead already names — sampling noise in a single 21-round median — rather than a threshold that is too strict. Doubling the rounds is the same intervention as candidate fix #1 (turn one noisy draw into an estimate) and it strengthens the control instead of loosening it: a tighter null makes clause 3 HARDER to pass by luck, not easier.

THE CHEAP TEST NEEDS NO CODE CHANGE. perf_harness.py:101 already reads ROUNDS from the environment:

  ROUNDS = int(os.environ.get("FNX_PERF_ROUNDS", "21"))

So the first experiment on this bead is not a gate edit at all. Re-run the p80x1.14 minimum_branching demonstration, unchanged, with FNX_PERF_ROUNDS=41, 8 independent repetitions as before, and count clause-3 vetoes. If they go from 2/8 to 0/8 with the same effect, the defect is round count and the fix is a default change with no clause redesign and no loosening — and the blocking predicate's WIN/LOSE table becomes much easier to argue, because raising rounds cannot preferentially admit wins.

If vetoes persist at 41 rounds, that result kills the cheap explanation and the clause redesign is warranted on its own terms. Either way it is one measurement against three candidate redesigns.

ON THE BLOCKING PREDICATE, flagged because it may be unreachable as written. It requires running the full claim-incumbent suite twice on this host. Every suite-level perf_harness invocation attempted by this fleet recently has failed the host-wide quiescence admission — see br-r37-c1-3s8x7, where SnowyValley recorded NO ADMISSIBLE MEASUREMENT after 25 attempts and diagnosed the gate as a per-CPU MAX that refuses at one-minute loads under 2 on a 64-way host. If that still holds, this bead is blocked behind the same admission problem it is trying to make less fragile. Two ways out worth considering, neither of which weakens the predicate: run the two suite passes in a genuinely reserved host window (the coordinated exclusive window SnowyValley asked five peers for and never got), or satisfy the predicate on a recorded replay of previously captured per-row null and candidate samples, re-deciding them offline under both clause variants — the WIN/LOSE split is computable from stored samples without re-running the workloads at all, if the harness's provenance retains them.

Nothing here changes the bead's disposition or its predicate; do not read it as licence to land a clause change.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CORRECTION TO MY OWN PRIOR COMMENT (OliveDesert, 2026-08-08). I ran the experiment I proposed. It does NOT support the claim I made, and the first version of it was confounded by my own design. Both are recorded here.

WHAT I TESTED. CoralIsland's exact fixture — minimum_branching, n=800/m=4000/seed=11 ordered-arc directed, weights 1..20, 800 nodes and 0 edges out, parity asserted before timing — at R=21 and R=41, dual A/A nulls per repetition, MAX_NULL_MEDIAN_BIAS held at 0.02, taskset -c 40-43 to match the demonstration. Script: scratchpad/rounds_vs_clause3.py.

FIRST RUN, WHICH I AM DISCARDING AS CONFOUNDED. All six R=21 repetitions ran first, then all six R=41. Result looked decisive: 4/6 vetoes at R=21 against 1/6 at R=41. It is not usable. Host load fell steadily across the invocation, so the R=41 block simply ran in quieter conditions than the R=21 block. Blocked designs cannot separate round count from drift. I caught this before publishing it and re-ran interleaved.

SECOND RUN, INTERLEAVED, 8 repetitions, alternating which round-count goes first so drift hits both equally. Load fell from 93 to 30 across the run, and every repetition records the load it started at.

  R=21 clause-3 vetoes: 1/8      R=41 clause-3 vetoes: 1/8
  clause 1 passed 8/8 and clause 2 passed 8/8 at BOTH round counts.

SO THE VETO-COUNT CLAIM IS NOT CONFIRMED. Doubling rounds did not reduce how often clause 3 fired. My earlier comment said 2/8 to 0/8 would show the defect is round count; the honest answer at 8 repetitions is that it did not.

WHAT DID CHANGE, and it is not nothing. The worst-null-bias DISTRIBUTION tightened by about 2x:

  R=21 worst biases: 0.0046 0.0124 0.0129 0.0136 0.0177 0.0189 0.0194 0.1628   median 0.0157
  R=41 worst biases: 0.0023 0.0045 0.0046 0.0061 0.0091 0.0103 0.0109 0.0257   median 0.0076

Six of the eight R=21 draws sit between 0.012 and 0.019 — under the 0.02 ceiling but with almost no margin — while R=41 mostly sits below 0.010. So rounds do buy real headroom against the clause; there is just not enough of it, at these repetition counts, to change the pass/fail tally.

LOAD IS THE DOMINANT TERM, and that is the clearest thing here. Both vetoes in the interleaved run came from repetition 1, at load ~93, one at each round count (R=21 bias 0.1628, R=41 bias 0.0257). Every repetition from load 59 downward passed clause 3 at both round counts. CoralIsland saw 2/8 at load 8.22; I saw comparable or worse at loads 30-93. The clause is behaving like a contention detector, which is arguably what it is for.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE THREE CANDIDATE FIXES. Raising rounds alone is now the weakest of them on this evidence — it improves the margin but not the verdict. Pooling both arms' nulls, or judging bias relative to the effect, both act directly on the failure mode actually observed here, which is one arm's null wandering while the other stays flat (R=21 rep1: 0.8372 against 0.9976; R=41 rep1: 0.9743 against 1.0023). A pooled or effect-relative clause survives exactly that, and a round-count increase does not.

NOT A RATIO CLAIM, explicitly. My effect estimates ran 4.53-5.06x against CoralIsland's 4.28-4.45x at load 8.22, so contention inflated them. These runs are evidence about GATE BEHAVIOUR ONLY and must not be read as a minimum_branching ratio; publishing 5.0x from a host at load 30-93 would be exactly the proof-class inflation CoralIsland correctly refused. br-r37-c1-p80x1.14 stays unconverted and its README row still says no current admissible ratio.

The blocking predicate on this bead is untouched, and the disposition is unchanged.

comments.text:
CANDIDATE FIXES SCORED ON IDENTICAL DRAWS (OliveDesert, 2026-08-08). This is the useful follow-up to my correction above: rather than argue between the bead's three candidates, run them against the SAME repetitions so they are compared on one body of evidence.

SETUP. CoralIsland's exact fixture (minimum_branching, n=800/m=4000/seed=11, weights 1..20, 800 nodes and 0 edges out, parity asserted before timing), harness default R=21, dual A/A nulls per repetition, 20 repetitions, taskset -c 40-43, one-minute load 4.0-5.5 throughout — quieter than the demonstration's 8.22, so this is not a contention-stressed sample. Script: scratchpad/clause3_variants.py. Variants evaluated per repetition on the same draws:

  current  : max over arms of |null_median - 1|           <= 0.02
  pooled   : |median(all null ratios from BOTH arms) - 1| <= 0.02
  relative : worst arm bias <= 0.02 OR bias <= effect_deviation/10

RESULT

  current   vetoes  2/20
  pooled    vetoes  0/20
  relative  vetoes  0/20

The two current-vetoes are precisely the failure mode I described last comment — one arm wanders, the other stays flat:

  rep12  effect 4.964x  nulls 1.0232 / 0.9955   worst 0.0232  POOLED 0.0033  arm disagreement 0.0277
  rep14  effect 5.038x  nulls 0.9751 / 0.9940   worst 0.0249  POOLED 0.0060  arm disagreement 0.0189

Pooling collapses both to well inside the bound because the wander is in one arm only. That is the mechanism, not a coincidence of thresholds.

THE INTEGRITY QUESTION, WHICH IS THE ONLY ONE THAT MATTERS. A variant that admits more is a loosening unless the runs it admits were good measurements. Here that is checkable from the same data: compare the vetoed repetitions' EFFECTS against the 18 the current clause admitted.

  admitted effects (n=18): 4.555 - 5.012x, median 4.954x
  vetoed rep12: 4.964x  — sits mid-distribution, ~60th percentile of the admitted set
  vetoed rep14: 5.038x  — sits just ABOVE the admitted maximum, by 0.5%

So one vetoed run is indistinguishable from the admitted population and the other is marginally at its top edge. Neither is the kind of outlier whose discarding protects anything. Clause 3 threw away two measurements that agree with the eighteen it kept. That is the definition of a false veto, and it is the first direct evidence on this bead that the vetoes are false rather than merely inconvenient.

WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING.
  * This does NOT satisfy the blocking predicate. That requires the full claim-incumbent suite under both clauses with the WIN vs LOSE split of newly-decidable rows. One workload cannot produce that table, and a variant that admits only wins must still be reverted. Nothing here licenses landing a clause change.
  * Different harness: these draws come from the balanced-square substrate, not perf_harness.py. Same fixture and same clause arithmetic, different slot layout.
  * Untested under contention: this sample is load 4-5. My earlier interleaved run at load 30-93 saw worse null behaviour at both R=21 and R=41, and I have NOT scored the variants there. A variant that only works on a quiet host is not a fix for the problem this bead describes, which is explicitly about contended hosts.
  * 20 repetitions, one effect size, one workload. Pooling's failure mode — both arms biased the same direction, which pooling cannot see but the current clause also cannot see — is not exercised by this sample at all.

RECOMMENDATION, offered not decided. Pooled is the better of the two survivors: it is a smaller change than effect-relative, it has no free parameter (effect_deviation/10 is arbitrary and would need its own justification), and it fails safe in the case that actually threatens a verdict, which is both arms biased together. If someone takes this bead, score pooled against the stored suite samples rather than re-running workloads — the WIN/LOSE split the predicate demands is computable offline from retained per-row null and candidate samples, which is the cheapest route to closing this that I can see.

comments.text:
THE OFFLINE ROUTE I PROPOSED IS REAL BUT NOT YET EXECUTABLE — AND THAT HALVES THIS BEAD'S COST (OliveDesert, 2026-08-08). Checking my own proposal rather than leaving it as a suggestion.

WHAT I PROPOSED EARLIER: that the blocking predicate — run the full claim-incumbent suite under the current clause 3 and under a candidate clause 3, and report how many vetoed rows become decidable plus their WIN/LOSE split — might be satisfiable offline from stored per-row samples, "if the harness's provenance retains them". I never checked. Checked now.

HALF ONE, CONFIRMED: THE HARNESS ALREADY EMITS EXACTLY WHAT IS NEEDED. Every row in `benchmark_results_json` carries, alongside the medians and CIs, the RAW per-round sample lists (scripts/perf_harness.py, the results.append block):

    "ratio_samples":     cand.ratios
    "null_nx_samples":   null_nx.ratios
    "null_fnx_samples":  null_fnx.ratios

Those are the per-round ratios for the candidate AND both A/A nulls. Any clause-3 variant — pooled, effect-relative, or a redrawn-null scheme — is a pure function of those three lists. So the predicate's whole table, including the WIN/LOSE split of newly-decidable rows, is computable from an archived run with zero re-measurement and zero host-quiescence requirement. Nothing needs to be added to the harness.

HALF TWO, THE PROBLEM: NO RUN'S OUTPUT HAS BEEN RETAINED. `grep -rl ratio_samples tests/artifacts/ docs/ artifacts/` returns ZERO files. The `benchmark_results_json=` line goes to stdout and nobody has captured it into a committed artifact. So the offline route cannot be executed today — there is no data to re-decide.

WHAT THIS CHANGES, AND IT IS THE POINT. This bead has been treated as needing TWO admitted full-suite runs on a host that has not admitted one in weeks (br-r37-c1-3s8x7: 25 attempts, 0 admitted). It does not. It needs ONE admitted run whose stdout is saved. From that single capture, both clause variants can be scored offline, repeatedly, by anyone, forever — and so can any future variant, without further host time.

CONCRETE ASK, cheap enough to attach to unrelated work: whoever next gets an admitted claim-incumbent invocation for ANY reason should redirect or tee its stdout into a committed artifact rather than reading the summary and discarding it. That single act converts this bead from blocked-on-an-unreachable-gate to a desk exercise. It costs nothing beyond a shell redirect and it does not weaken any gate — the samples are what the harness already decided on.

I have not created that artifact myself: I cannot obtain an admitted run on this host, and fabricating one from my own balanced-square substrate would not be the harness's samples and must not be substituted for them.

Also worth noting for whoever does the scoring: the candidate variants are already implemented and validated against real draws in my earlier comment on this bead — current vetoes 2/20, pooled 0/20, effect-relative 0/20, with the two vetoed repetitions' effects sitting inside the admitted distribution. That comment supplies the arithmetic; this one supplies the data path.

SCORING TOOL COMMITTED — the analysis half of the blocking predicate is now a single command (OliveDesert, 2026-08-08). scripts/rescore_clause3.py.

The predicate needs two things: an admitted suite run, and the WIN/LOSE table computed from it. I cannot obtain the first on this host. The second is now done and committed, so whoever gets an admitted run for ANY reason needs only:

  python3 scripts/perf_harness.py claim-incumbent | tee artifacts/<run>.txt
  python3 scripts/rescore_clause3.py artifacts/<run>.txt

It re-decides every row under current vs a candidate clause 3, holding clauses 1 and 2 fixed so a row that flips can only have flipped because of clause 3, and prints exactly what the predicate asks: unchanged / newly decidable / of which WIN / of which LOSE / newly UNdecidable, with each flipped row's label and ratio. Both candidate variants from this bead are implemented (pooled, effect-relative).

VERIFIED on a synthetic fixture in the harness's emitted shape, containing one clause-3 veto that is a WIN and one that is a LOSS, both caused by the ONE-ARM wander this bead diagnoses. The tool reports 1 WIN and 1 LOSE flip and leaves the clean row unchanged — i.e. it can report a variant admitting losses as well as wins, which is the integrity property the predicate turns on. A tool that could only surface wins would be useless for this check.

It prints a standing reminder that a variant admitting ONLY wins is a loosening and must be reverted, and that the tool reports rather than decides.

WHAT IT DELIBERATELY WILL NOT DO: substitute other samples. It reads the harness's own ratio_samples / null_nx_samples / null_fnx_samples. Feeding it my balanced-square substrate's numbers would be proof-class substitution — the predicate exists so the decision rests on the harness's measurements, and I have not done that.

When I committed scripts/rescore_clause3.py I verified it on a synthetic fixture using --variant pooled only, while the tool ships TWO variants. Closing that gap in my own verification.

  --variant pooled     1 WIN flip, 1 LOSE flip, 1 unchanged
  --variant relative   1 WIN flip, 1 LOSE flip, 1 unchanged

                       benchmark_results_json= line; no traceback

No defect. Both code paths run, both report flips in BOTH directions, and the error path tells the user what to capture rather than dumping a JSONDecodeError.

So the fixture is a SMOKE TEST — it proves each variant runs and can surface losses as well as wins — and NOT a discrimination test. It does not show the variants differ, and nothing here bears on which of them should be preferred.

Choosing between them still needs the real suite samples. My earlier comment on this bead scored them against 20 real draws (current 2/20 vetoes, pooled 0/20, relative 0/20) and argued pooled is the better survivor on grounds of being the smaller change with no free parameter — RELATIVE_K = 10.0 in the tool is arbitrary and would need its own justification before anyone relied on the relative arm.

comments.author: SunnyTern
comments.text:
A SECOND, INDEPENDENT DEMONSTRATION OF CLAUSE-3 VERDICT INSTABILITY — AND ONE CANDIDATE REMEDY TESTED AND REFUTED (SunnyTern, 2026-08-09). No source change. Bead stays OPEN; its blocking predicate (the full claim-incumbent suite under both clause-3 variants, with the win/lose split published) is untouched and still governs.

WHY THIS IS WORTH ADDING. This bead's demonstration is minimum_branching: a stable 4.28-4.45x effect, clause 3 vetoing 2 of 8 runs, null medians 0.9574-0.9772, i.e. bias 0.023-0.043. I hit the same class from a different surface today — graph.copy() arms measured against live nx 3.6.1 — and it behaves the same way but with much larger swings, which matters for how the candidate fixes must be validated.

VERDICT MOVED WITH NO CODE CHANGE, same binary, same host band, two runs ~30 minutes apart:

  MultiGraph.copy()   run A  nulls 0.6715 / 0.6748  UNDECIDABLE   (ratio 2.1200)
                      run B  nulls 1.0011 / 1.0032  ADMISSIBLE    (ratio 2.3134)
  MultiDiGraph.copy() run A  nulls 1.0023 / 0.9486  UNDECIDABLE   (ratio 2.6102)
                      run B  nulls 1.1329 / 1.1996  UNDECIDABLE   (ratio 2.7741)
  Graph.copy()        run A  nulls 1.5550 / 1.3397  UNDECIDABLE   (ratio 6.2023)
                      run B  nulls 0.9528 / 0.9438  UNDECIDABLE   (ratio 5.4523)

The ratios are stable across runs (2.12/2.31, 2.61/2.77, 6.20/5.45) while the nulls swing from 0.67 to 1.00 on the SAME row. That is this bead's complaint reproduced on an unrelated surface.

BUT THERE ARE TWO DISTINCT FAILURE POPULATIONS, and conflating them would break the fix. The minimum_branching vetoes are sampling noise in a single median — bias 0.02-0.04. The copy arms are GENUINELY non-stationary — bias 0.06 to 0.55 — because each slot allocates and frees a whole graph, so the heap moves under the measurement. Clause 3 is doing its job on the second population and should keep refusing it.

THAT IS A CONSTRAINT ON THIS BEAD'S CANDIDATE FIXES, specifically the third one. "Require the null's bias to be small RELATIVE to the candidate's effect" would admit MultiGraph.copy run A: bias 0.33 against an effect deviation of 1.12 is proportionally modest, yet that measurement really is broken. Whoever implements the relative test must check it against a genuinely non-stationary arm, not only against minimum_branching. The re-draw and pooling variants look safer on this evidence because they attack the sampling-noise population without loosening the absolute bound.

A CANDIDATE REMEDY I TESTED AND IT FAILED — recorded so nobody re-derives it. A blocked/paired estimator is the textbook answer to a drifting arm: the ABBA layout already contains adjacent (a,b) couples, so take per-couple ratios and median those, and drift that moves both arms between couples cancels inside each ratio. Implemented, with the null built from the only same-arm adjacencies the layout contains (positions 1,2 are (b,b) and 3,4 are (a,a) — pairing arbitrary same-arm slots would compare across the block and measure drift the paired estimator never sees).

  row                unpaired nulls        paired nulls        paired ratio / unpaired
  Graph.copy         0.9528 / 0.9438      0.9922 / 1.3178     5.7802 / 5.4523
  MultiGraph.copy    1.0011 / 1.0032      0.9656 / 1.0662     2.2707 / 2.3134
  MultiDiGraph.copy  1.1329 / 1.1996      1.0558 / 1.0741     2.7191 / 2.7741

The paired ratios agree with the unpaired ones to within a few percent, so the estimator is not wrong — but its nulls are WORSE on two of three rows and it turned an ADMISSIBLE row (MultiGraph) into an undecidable one. The likely reason is sample count: each round yields exactly one same-arm couple per arm, so the paired null is a median over 15 values against the unpaired null's 60. Pairing buys drift cancellation and pays for it in null resolution, and on this evidence the trade is not worth making. Do not add a paired estimator to the harness on the strength of the textbook argument alone.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY HELP THE SECOND POPULATION, offered rather than claimed: stop the arm from being non-stationary instead of estimating around it — a fresh subprocess per slot, or an arm shape that does not allocate whole graphs per timed unit. That is the shared blocker behind the UNDECIDABLE rows on br-r37-c1-jc9e4 (add_edge, refused 3 of 4 attempts) and br-r37-c1-yl606 (copy), and fixing it unblocks several claim rows at once.

comments.author: SunnyTern
comments.text:
SUBPROCESS-PER-SLOT SUBSTRATE — THE UNDECIDABLE ROWS ADMIT (SunnyTern, 2026-08-09). No source change.

THE PROBLEM, recorded three times today from three angles: add_edge (jc9e4, refused 3 of 4 attempts), copy (yl606, refused 5 of 6), and the second failure population on d4xot. All the same cause — each timed slot allocates and frees whole graphs, so the heap moves under the measurement and the A/A null reads that drift rather than the arm. Estimating around it FAILED: a blocked/paired estimator agreed on the ratio but made the nulls worse.

THE FIX removes the cause instead of estimating around it. Every timed slot runs in its OWN process, so each starts from an identical fresh heap and the arm is stationary by construction. Interpreter startup and fixture construction are NOT timed — the worker times only the inner work and prints nanoseconds — so ~0.5 s of process setup stays out of the measurement. The balanced [A B B A A B B A] order and the dual A/A nulls are unchanged, so a row that admits here admits on the same terms as every other row this session.

MEASURED, live networkx 3.6.1, extension built from HEAD (_fnx.abi3.so sha256 016b512e35fe25979fb29aa5c649701eb79a8acbd6cba21520c68b57afe85e87), taskset -c 40-47, host load ~70 of 64:

  add_edge (fresh Graph, 8000 edges)
    run 1   0.8990x  CI95 [0.8885, 0.9137]   nulls 0.9837 / 1.0026   ADMISSIBLE
    run 2   0.8997x  CI95 [0.8859, 0.9168]   nulls 1.0006 / 0.9744   UNDECIDABLE

  MultiDiGraph.copy()
            3.7843x  CI95 [3.7297, 3.8416]   nulls 0.9877 / 1.0144   ADMISSIBLE

Compare the in-process substrate on the same rows: add_edge refused three times with estimates scattered 0.9291-0.9663, and MultiDiGraph.copy refused twice. Here the two add_edge point estimates agree to 0.001 and one run admits outright.

CAVEAT, AND IT IS NOT COSMETIC: a fresh process per slot removes drift but CHANGES WHAT IS MEASURED. Every slot now pays cold-heap costs — page faults, allocator warm-up — that a long-running program pays once. Both arms pay it equally so the ratio is fair, but the absolute figures are higher (fnx 1161 ns/edge here against 1030-1050 in-process) and the ratio is not identical to a warm steady-state ratio (0.899 here against 0.93-0.97 in-process). Quote it as what it is: the fresh-process build ratio. A steady-state ratio needs the in-process substrate and therefore still needs the drift problem solved another way.

WHAT IT COSTS: 120 subprocess launches per row, about two minutes. That is cheap against a row that has been undecidable for a day.

title: fix(node_key_to_string): integer node keys wider than i64 collapse into one node
description:
MEASURED on HEAD 98066b4b1 (PYTHONPATH=python, live nx 3.6.1):

  G.add_nodes_from([2**63-1, 2**63, 2**63+1, 2**64, 2**64+1, -(2**64)])
  nx  -> 6 nodes
  fnx -> 5 nodes    (silent DATA LOSS)

ROOT CAUSE, crates/fnx-python/src/lib.rs node_key_to_string. A Python int that
fails extract::<i64>() is WIDER than i64, but it then falls into the f64 branch:
extract::<f64>() SUCCEEDS with a rounded value (2**63+7 and 2**63+8 both round to
2f64.powi(63)), the branch's bound is 'f <= i64::MAX as f64' -- and 'i64::MAX as
f64' rounds UP to 2**63, so 2**63 itself passes -- and 'f as i64' then SATURATES
to i64::MAX. Every wide int in that window canonicalizes to the single string
'9223372036854775807', which is also the canonical of the DISTINCT key 2**63-1.

Two separable defects:
 (a) wide ints must never enter the float branch: their repr is the exact decimal;
 (b) the integral-float bound must be strictly below 2**63 so 'f as i64' cannot
     saturate onto a real key.

Reproduces on add_edge, on a sub-threshold add_edges_from (below
PLAIN_EDGE_BATCH_MIN=8, so no native batch), and on add_nodes_from -- it is the
canonicalization function, not a batch artifact.

TESTS THE FIX MUST CARRY: i64::MIN/i64::MAX boundary keys stay distinct from
their +/-1 neighbours; 2**63-1 / 2**63 / 2**63+1 are three nodes; negative wide
keys; edges between two wide keys keep both endpoints; int-vs-str keys stay
distinct; and 1/1.0/True still COLLAPSE (the negative case a fix that simply
routed every int through repr would break, since repr(True)=='True').
close_reason: Fixed in 5b0bc635d: wide Python int node keys and MultiGraph edge keys now canonicalize to their exact decimal via unbound int.__repr__, and the integral-float bound is exclusive at 2**63. Three new parity tests fail on the pre-fix ELF and pass on the fixed one; a fourth locks the hash-equal collapse that a naive repr-everything fix would break.

title: fix(bellman_ford): emit path/length dicts in networkx SPFA discovery order
description: single_source_bellman_ford{,_path,_path_length} and all_pairs_bellman_ford_path Python wrappers still reorder via _reorder_by_distance(G=,source=) which uses BFS-from-source hop order as the tie-break. nx's bellman-ford yields dicts in SPFA processing order (built from the predecessor dict in discovery order), which diverges from BFS-hop on equal-distance ties. Probe: key-order mismatch ~66% (157/236) on random weighted graphs. Fix mirrors br-r37-c1-k9q6q: have the Rust SPFA kernel (bellman_ford_spfa, added in br-r37-c1-wloxg) record enqueue/discovery order, return order-preserving Vec<(node,val)>, and have the Python bellman wrappers trust kernel order (stable sort by distance) instead of BFS. NOTE: _reorder_by_distance is shared with dijkstra (already fixed to call it without G/source) — keep bellman's order source-of-truth in the kernel.
close_reason: Bellman-Ford SPFA kernel now records first-discovery order; single_source_bellman_ford{,_path,_path_length}{,_directed} + single_source_bellman_ford + all_pairs_bellman_ford_path{,_length} return order-preserving Vec<(node,val)>. Python wrappers trust kernel discovery order directly (NOT distance-sorted) instead of BFS-hop reorder. Verified 0 key-order mismatches across 2622 single-source + 400 all_pairs + 2702 negative-weight instances (directed+undirected), values + cycle detection intact; 151 new regression tests + full 19433-test suite pass.

comments.author: CrimsonBeaver
comments.text:
CLOSING ON CITED EVIDENCE — the named probe passes on a build containing the cache (CrimsonBeaver, 2026-08-14).

The traverse fix is in HEAD: 'git show HEAD:crates/fnx-python/src/lib.rs | grep -c edge_py_attrs_by_endpoint.values()' returns 1, i.e. traverse_python_refs now visits the endpoint lookaside alongside edge_py_attrs, matching what clear_python_refs already cleared.

NAMED PROBE, run on ELF 1c227992ec84e56e built from the current tree (which carries the edge_py_attrs_by_endpoint cache):

  tests/python/test_view_descriptor_parity.py::test_direct_edge_attribute_self_reference_is_stored_and_collectable
  -> 4 passed

That is the exact test that failed 1/55104 on the build where the cache existed without the traverse, so it discriminates: it fails with the asymmetry present and passes with it removed.

GENERAL RULE THIS LEAVES BEHIND, worth more than the fix: any new field on PyGraph/PyDiGraph/PyMultiGraph/PyMultiDiGraph holding a Py<...> must be added to traverse_python_refs and clear_python_refs TOGETHER. CPython requires tp_traverse and tp_clear to cover the same references; a reference that is cleared but not traversed is invisible to the cycle collector and leaks silently. It costs nothing at the call site and only surfaces under a cycle, which is why one narrow self-reference test was the only thing in 55k cases that caught it.

REACHED CODE, verified not assumed: G.edges on a simple Graph returns the NATIVE EdgeView (type(g.edges) is _fnx.EdgeView -> True), so EdgeView::__getitem__ at crates/fnx-python/src/views.rs is the code under test. Note DiGraph/MultiGraph/MultiDiGraph do NOT use the native EdgeView, so this row is Graph-only.

ALREADY DONE AND NOT THE ANSWER, do not redo it: the two owned endpoint canonical Strings were removed from this exact function (borrowed stack-buffer probe, br-r37-c1-ey6ob, 2026-08-14). Exact allocation census before/after showed the (u,v) in G.edges() sibling drop 3.015 allocs/op against a 0.016 control, while G.edges[u,v] itself moved only 0.016/op — i.e. the canonicalization allocations were NOT its cost.

WHERE TO LOOK NEXT, unprofiled: the residue is materialize_edge_py_attrs (crates/fnx-python/src/lib.rs:2499), which calls Self::edge_key(left, right) -> (u.to_owned(), v.to_owned()) — TWO heap Strings allocated purely to entry()-probe the edge_py_attrs HashMap, including on the hit path. std HashMap has no borrowed tuple-key probe, so removing it needs either a single-String canonical edge key or a scratch buffer reused across calls. That is a lib.rs change and is the obvious first candidate, but it is a READING, not a profile.

METHOD NOTE: Ir is the wrong instrument on this surface. Importing the 2.4MB python/franken_networkx/__init__.py costs ~3.3e9 instructions with ~4e7 of run-to-run jitter, as large as a 20000-op loop; the baseline subtraction produced NEGATIVE per-op counts. title: fix(backend): backend_priority mode recurses forever on 4 dispatchable algorithms
description:
The README's documented drop-in mode (nx.config.backend_priority = ["franken_networkx"]) makes four algorithms recurse until RecursionError. scripts/verify_docs.py fails on README block 12 because of it, so the docs gate has been red on a real product bug.

REPRO (executed on a9ecce9c3):
  import networkx as nx; nx.config.backend_priority = ["franken_networkx"]
  import franken_networkx as fnx
  fnx.community.louvain_communities(nx.path_graph(200), seed=7)   -> RecursionError

TWO DISTINCT CAUSES, found by sweeping all 316 entries of _SUPPORTED_ALGORITHMS:

(1) louvain_communities. community.py:301 falls back to _nx_community.louvain_communities(...)
    WITHOUT backend="networkx". With backend_priority set, nx routes that call straight back into
    our backend, which falls back again. tournament.py:120 already pins backend="networkx" - that
    is the established idiom in this package and louvain simply missed it.

(2) max_clique / maximum_independent_set / clique_removal. backend.py:200-202 register
    fnx.approximation.<name>, and approximation.py obtains those names from a wildcard
    re-export of networkx.algorithms.approximation - so the registered 'implementation' IS nx's own
    @_dispatchable of the same name. Dispatch is a pure cycle with no fnx code in it at all.
    Pinning does NOT fix these: nx's max_clique body calls clique_removal() unpinned, so the cycle
    re-forms one frame deeper. The registration itself is the defect - there is no native kernel
    behind these three names.

BUG CLASS (statically detectable): an entry of _SUPPORTED_ALGORITHMS whose implementation
__module__ starts with 'networkx'. Exactly 3 of 316 entries qualify, and they are exactly the three
above.
close_reason: Fixed in 64ccd8144. Sweep under backend_priority went from 4 recursing algorithms of 316 registered to 0 of 313; louvain's nx fallback now pins backend='networkx' and the three approximation names that registered nx's own dispatchable as our implementation are deregistered (verified nx-identical on both nx and fnx graphs). Locked by tests/python/test_backend_dispatch_cycles.py, 11 passed, verified to fail when either cause is reintroduced.

comments.author: ProudBasin
comments.text:
ProudBasin: EVIDENCE CORRECTION (fleet-wide verification bug). My 'ubs ... exit 0' was obtained with an unsound idiom; re-verified properly, conclusion HOLDS.

THE DEFECT: I ran 'ubs <files> 2>&1 | tail -15; echo "ubs_exit=$?"'. A pipeline reports its LAST
command's status, so that printed TAIL's exit code - 0 no matter what ubs found.

RE-VERIFIED UNPIPED on the same three files:
    ubs python/franken_networkx/backend.py python/franken_networkx/community.py \
        tests/python/test_backend_dispatch_cycles.py > <file> 2>&1 ; echo $?
    UBS_TRUE_EXIT=0
    Critical: 0
    Warning: 2
So the claim holds exactly as published.

WHAT WAS ALREADY SOUND, and worth separating: the '0 critical / 2 warnings' half never depended on
the exit status - I read those from ubs's own printed summary lines. Reading a tool's own report is
a direct signal; inferring from $? after a pipe is not. Every later ubs check I ran this session
used the 'ubs ... | grep -E "Critical:|Warning:"' form, which reads the summary rather than the
status, so those are unaffected.

ALSO CHECKED, since the same idiom could have corrupted the perf evidence: my measurement drivers
capture the harness status as
    taskset -c 0-3 python3 scripts/perf_harness.py "$suite" > "$out" 2>&1
    rc=$?
- a REDIRECT, not a pipe, with $? taken immediately. So all six admitted br-r37-c1-oe93x arms and
every recorded refusal rest on a true exit status. That was the claim I most needed to be sure of.

title: test: Gallai's identity (matching + edge cover = n) + validity
description: Gallai's theorem nu(G)+rho(G)=|V| (max matching cardinality + min edge cover cardinality = n, no isolated vertices) cross-checks two independent algorithms + node count; cardinality parity vs nx; min_edge_cover validity (covers every node); matching disjointness validity. Oracle-free theorem invariant. ~80 cases.
close_reason: FIRST, A CHECK THAT CAME BACK CLEAN: I picked this bead hunting the defect I found on br-r37-c1-z0f6q - a claimed identity whose two sides are the same expression computed by two libraries. Gallai here is NOT that. nu comes from max_weight_matching, rho from min_edge_cover, and they are compared against |V|, which is three genuinely independent quantities. The identity is real and I am recording that it checked out rather than manufacturing a problem with it. THE ACTUAL GAP, the same one that has now appeared on six consecutive beads: the sweep asserts only CARDINALITIES. Nothing required the cover or the matching to be built from G edges, and matching disjointness is asserted on cycle_graph(6) alone - so on the entire 40-draw random family, a matching of NON-ADJACENT pairs or a cover using edges absent from G satisfies every assertion. Both are now required to come from G (35/35 verified before writing), and disjointness is asserted on every draw rather than one named graph. Added irredundancy of the cover: dropping any single edge must leave some node uncovered. That is a necessary condition of MINIMALITY which the size comparison does not imply on its own - a cover of the right size could still contain a redundant edge if it also omitted a needed one, and the node-coverage check alone would not see the redundancy. Verified 35/35. THE SKIP HID A CONTRACT: both sweeps skip graphs with an isolated vertex, 5 of 40 draws, and simply discard them. What actually happens there is a documented refusal - a node with no incident edge cannot be covered, so min_edge_cover raises NetworkXException in fnx and in live networkx 3.6.1 alike. That is now pinned instead of skipped. Evidence: file 80 -> 107 passed + 15 skipped (the 15 are the same 5 isolated-vertex draws now appearing across three sweeps rather than two; the underlying skip rate is unchanged at 5/40); 214 passed + 15 skipped across the matching/cover family (matching_coloring_closed_forms, maximal_matching_bound, matching). Crate-scoped and inline with a timeout cap; no background jobs left running. Committed 83f0d832e, pushed to main then master separately after a fast-forward check. Test-only, no Rust touched, no CGSE surface.

title: test: tree algorithms (Prufer bijection + spanning-tree invariants)
description: Prufer sequence bijection (encode->decode->encode identity) + from_prufer nx parity + is_tree/n-1-edges, MST/maxST weight parity + invariants (n-1 edges, is_tree, maxST>=MST). 80 cases.
close_reason: A WEIGHT TOTAL DOES NOT SAY THE EDGES CAME FROM G. The spanning-tree coverage was three things: the edge count, is_tree, and a summed weight matching networkx. A tree assembled from edges that are NOT in the input, carrying weights that happen to total correctly, satisfies all three - the same defect class as the maximal-matching bead (br-r37-c1-rqau5), where disjointness and maximality were satisfiable by pairs that were not edges. Both trees now must span G node set exactly, use only G edges, and carry G weight on each edge rather than an invented one - verified 35/35 on the connected draws before asserting. THE INEQUALITY: maxST >= MST is satisfied by equality, so a family where the two never separate would make it vacuous. I measured rather than assumed - they separate STRICTLY on 35 of 35 connected draws - but I deliberately did NOT assert strictness as a law, because equality is legitimate when all weights are equal. The guard asserts the FAMILY separates them on all but a few draws, which is the honest form: it protects the inequality from going vacuous without claiming something false about graphs in general. PRUFER BOUNDARIES: the sweep draws sequences of length n-2 for n in 3..12, so the ends are unreachable by construction. Added the empty sequence for a 2-node tree (returns the single edge), an out-of-range value (NetworkXError), encoding a non-tree (NotATree), and encoding a 2-node tree (empty sequence) - all four compared against live networkx 3.6.1 by outcome, and all four agree. Evidence: file 80 -> 115 passed + 10 skipped (the 10 are the 5 disconnected draws now appearing in two sweeps rather than one; the pre-existing sweep already skipped 5); 653 passed + 10 skipped across the tree/MST family (prufer_sequence_parity, tree_structural_invariants, mst_return_type_parity). Crate-scoped and inline with a timeout cap; no background jobs left running. Committed 9ae26feff, pushed to main then master separately after a fast-forward check. Test-only, no Rust touched, no CGSE surface.

title: MultiDiGraph weighted degree: full nx parity blocked by per-edge string-keyed store lookup
description: Shipped ac98e77d4 (br-r37-c1-mdgwdeg): Rust-store int weighted-degree path moved MultiDiGraph in/out/total degree(weight) from 0.41-0.54x to 0.78-0.95x vs NetworkX (cargo-bench confirmed). RESIDUAL structural blocker to full (>=1.0x) parity: the store path still does a per-edge string-keyed edge_attrs(u,v,key) HashMap lookup (String hashing per edge), whereas nx iterates pure-C _succ[n]/_pred[n] dicts. Closing fully needs an INDEX-NATIVE per-node weight accumulator in fnx-classes MultiDiGraph (iterate edges by node index summing CgseValue::Int weights without string round-trips), e.g. a weighted_in/out_degree_by_index(attr) -> i64 method using the integer CSR adjacency. Until then 0.78-0.88x is the floor for the string-keyed approach. Do NOT re-derive; this bead is the record.
notes: REFUTED as a perf lever (cc 2026-06-25, see docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md). Built the proposed index-native MultiDiGraph::weighted_degree_int_accumulate (single edges-map pass, no per-key edge_attrs re-lookup, ~half the Rust-side hashing). Per-crate Criterion bench: fnx side STATISTICALLY UNCHANGED (in_degree 3.153->3.177ms within CI; out 2.576->2.579ms). The floor is NOT the string-keyed edge_attrs lookup — it is the PyObject materialization of the degree view (1800 nodes x py_node_key + into_py_any), identical on both paths. NO-SHIP/reverted (stash cc-eilce-NOSHIP). Closing the gap needs cutting per-node Python-object construction, not the edge walk.

title: add_edge that implicitly creates nodes didn't bump nodes_seq (regression from br-r37-c1-39d82)
description:
After landing the nodes_seq mutation counter (br-r37-c1-39d82), discovered that add_edge methods that implicitly create nodes (via node_key_map.entry().or_insert_with()) didn't bump nodes_seq. So an iterator over G that calls G.add_edge(existing_u, new_v) during iteration would miss the 'dictionary changed size during iteration' error required by Python's dict iter contract.

Fix: at the top of each add_edge (4 sites: PyGraph, PyMultiGraph, PyDiGraph, PyMultiDiGraph), record __was_new = !node_key_map.contains_key(u) || !node_key_map.contains_key(v) BEFORE the .entry().or_insert_with() inserts. After the inserts, conditionally bump if __was_new. add_edges_from / add_weighted_edges_from / etc all delegate to add_edge, so the fix cascades.

Verified:
- All 4 classes detect implicit-new-node add_edge (raises RuntimeError)
- All 4 classes do NOT raise on add_edge with both endpoints already in the graph
- 17506 Python tests pass

title: fix: double_edge_swap inflates max_tries by nswap factor — diverges from nx
description: fnx.double_edge_swap at python/franken_networkx/__init__.py:24224 computes max_attempts = nswap * max_tries, but nx caps total tries at exactly max_tries (loop body uses 'if n >= max_tries' in networkx/algorithms/swap.py:222). title: test: betweenness centrality closed forms + normalization relationship
description: Betweenness closed forms: K_n all-zero (no intermediaries), star center=1/leaves=0, path-middle maximal/endpoints=0, non-negativity, normalized<=1, unnormalized=normalized*(n-1)(n-2)/2. Oracle-free closed-form + cross-parameter invariants. 37 cases.
close_reason: The file's normalization relation is the UNDIRECTED one and no digraph was ever tested. All pre-existing tests build Graph / star / path / complete, so directed coverage was 0 draws. On a digraph an ordered pair (s,t) and its reverse are distinct, so the scale is (n-1)(n-2) with no halving. MEASURED: the directed scale holds 30/30 and the file's undirected scale holds 0/30 - the relation as written is simply false for digraphs. MUTANT, two figures reported honestly rather than the flattering one: a normalization applying the undirected /2 scale to digraphs is caught by the exact scale assertion on 30/30 draws (that is the assertion I actually wrote); the weaker secondary symptom, normalized values exceeding 1, shows on only 3/30, so a test asserting only the <=1 bound would have missed it 27 times. Added: the directed scale relation with an explicit assertion that the halved scale does NOT hold wherever betweenness is nonzero; non-negativity and <=1 on digraphs; a guard test asserting at least 20 of 30 digraphs have nonzero betweenness, since the scale relation is trivially satisfied where every value is 0; the  parameter, which changes the DEFINITION rather than the scale - counting a node on the pairs it terminates adds exactly (n-1) to its unnormalized score, verified 21/21 on the connected draws and gated on connectivity because the identity needs all pairs reachable, with monotonicity (endpoints=True >= endpoints=False) asserted unconditionally at 30/30; and a path witness where the endpoints intermediate nothing so only  can lift them off zero. Left alone deliberately: edge_betweenness_centrality (a sibling function this bead does not name) and the k-sampling parameter (randomized). Evidence: file 37 -> 99 passed, no skips; 227 passed across the centrality family (centrality_metric_invariants, current_flow_centrality_parity). Crate-scoped, not a workspace run. Test-only, no Rust touched, no CGSE surface.

title: perf(classes): add_edge writes two near-identical ledger records per edge — record the gate decision only when it refuses
description:
Follow-up to br-r37-c1-8n3j3. All four edge-add hot paths (Graph::add_edge_with_attrs,
MultiGraph::add_edge_impl, DiGraph::add_edge_with_attrs, MultiDiGraph::add_edge_impl) call
record_decision to OBTAIN the gate action, then call it again at the end with the outcome
evidence. On the allow path that writes two records with the same operation, mode, action and
incompatibility_probability, the second carrying strictly richer evidence (self_loop,
edge_attr_count, left/right_autocreated vs just unknown_incompatible_feature).

Measured cost of the pair after the residency bound landed: 353.5 ns/edge of retention +
140.8 ns/edge of evidence construction + 50.9 ns/edge of clock reads, i.e. 21.3% of
add_edge_with_attrs, for 2 records/edge. Halving the record count is the largest remaining term
and is a ~10-line change confined to fnx-classes.

title: PERF-5 in-flight edges_dirty impl: 3 defects (Cell-not-Sync compile blocker + missing initializers + incomplete handout instrumentation -> lost mutations)
description:
A peer is mid-edit (working-tree, uncommitted) on br-r37-c1-g5ifq, adding edges_dirty to skip the F1 weight-sync. Gauntlet differential review found 3 defects BEFORE it lands:

(1) COMPILE BLOCKER: edges_dirty is declared 'Cell<bool>' (lib.rs:325/414, digraph.rs:41/63). PyO3 #[pyclass] requires Sync; Cell<bool> is NOT Sync (digraph.rs:29 error E0277 'Cell<bool> cannot be shared between threads safely'). fnx releases the GIL via py.allow_threads, so graph pyclasses MUST be Sync. Use std::sync::atomic::AtomicBool with Ordering::Relaxed instead of Cell<bool> (.load()/.store() replace .get()/.set()).

(2) COMPILE BLOCKER: ~9 PyGraph {..} struct initializers in crates/fnx-python/src/algorithms.rs (lines ~12829,12877,13007,13036,13124,13234,13258,13653,13701) are missing the new edges_dirty field (E0063). Every PyGraph/PyDiGraph/PyMultiGraph/PyMultiDiGraph initializer needs edges_dirty: AtomicBool::new(true_or_false).

(3) CORRECTNESS (lost mutations): edges_dirty is set true at only 4 sites (lib.rs:1311,3079; digraph.rs:898,3304 — the adjacency __getitem__). But edge-attr dicts are ALSO handed out (mutably) via: EdgeView.__getitem__ (G.edges[u,v], views.rs — NO edges_dirty write found), edges(data=True) iteration (views.rs AllData path), AdjacencyView access (G.adj[u][v]), and possibly get_edge_data. A user doing 'for u,v,d in G.edges(data=True): d["weight"]=5' or 'G.edges[u,v]["weight"]=5' on a fresh (edges_dirty=false) graph then a weighted algorithm would SILENTLY get the unsynced (wrong) result. ALL edge-dict handout sites must set edges_dirty=true (incl. views.rs EdgeView/AdjacencyView/data-iteration), or use the behavior-identical alternative: skip replace_edge_attrs only when py_dict.is_empty() AND inner.edge_attrs(u,v) is empty/None (no flag needed, no lost-mutation risk — see br-r37-c1-0ls6k). VERIFY with: fresh generator graph, mutate one edge weight via EACH handout path, run dijkstra/pagerank, compare to nx.

title: to_scipy_sparse_array / to_numpy_array: 15-19x slower than nx (PyO3 per-edge cost)
description:
fnx.to_scipy_sparse_array (alias of adjacency_matrix) ran 4.92ms vs nx 0.35ms on a 100-node 1k-edge digraph (15x slower); fnx.to_numpy_array 4.39ms vs nx 0.23ms (19x slower). Both are hot paths for hits, katz_centrality_numpy, laplacian_matrix, normalized_laplacian_matrix, and effective_graph_resistance.

Root cause: both iterated G.edges(data=True), which materializes (u, v, attrs) tuples one-at-a-time across PyO3 (~3.5ms for 1000 edges, dominating the wrapper budget).

Fix: switch the non-multigraph paths to G._adj.items() — yields (u, dict_of_v_to_attrs) directly, saving the per-edge tuple alloc. For undirected graphs this means each edge is visited twice (once from each endpoint) so the natural symmetric population happens without an explicit u != v reverse-write branch.

Measured: to_numpy_array 4.39 -> 3.23ms (~25% faster); to_scipy_sparse_array 4.92 -> 4.42ms (~10% faster); hits 7.30 -> 5.78ms (~20% faster).

Still 9-12x slower than nx — the residual gap is the fundamental PyO3 round-trip cost of materialising N attrs dicts. Closing it requires a Rust-native batch helper that emits the COO arrays directly (filed as follow-up: br-r37-c1-tssa-rustnative).

Caught a latent bug in the process: I initially still emitted the symmetric (v, u) reverse-write in _adj.items() loops, which double-emits each undirected edge, summing in scipy COO and yielding effective_graph_resistance(K_2) = 0.5 instead of 1.0. Fixed before committing.
notes: Partial fix in same commit. _adj.items() path saves 20-25% across to_numpy_array / to_scipy_sparse_array / hits. Residual gap (~9-12x of nx) is fundamental PyO3 attrs-dict cost; closing it requires a Rust-native batch helper (see br-r37-c1-tssa-rustnative).
